title: Effect of post-exercise sauna bathing on the endurance performance of competitive male runners
authors: Scoon GS, Hopkins WG, Mayhew S, Cotter JD
journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
findings: In a cross-over design, 3 weeks of sitting in a humid sauna at about 90 C straight after training (31 +/- 5 min, on 12.7 +/- 2.1 occasions) was compared with 3 weeks of control training, with a 3 week washout.

Run time to exhaustion at the runner's best 5 km speed was 32% longer after the sauna period (90% confidence limits 21-43%), about 1.9% in a time trial; this was a cool-condition treadmill test, not a test in the heat.

Plasma volume rose 7.1% (5.6-8.7%) and red-cell volume 3.5% (-0.8 to 8.1%) after the sauna period; the change in performance correlated with the change in plasma volume (r 0.96) and in total blood volume (r 0.94).
The authors conclude that 3 weeks of post-exercise sauna bathing gave a worthwhile gain in endurance running performance, probably through blood volume.
limitations: Six men; the outcome was run time to exhaustion in temperate conditions and blood volume, not heat tolerance, core temperature or performance in the heat, so the study shows a training effect of post-exercise heat and not heat acclimation as such; the sauna was about 90 C for about 30 min, a hotter and longer exposure than a home sauna session for many people; women and non-competitive runners were not studied. Abstract read on Europe PMC; the full text was not read.
implications: Supports a sauna straight after a run as a passive heat exposure of a competitive runner's training: about 30 min, on most days of 3 weeks; it does not show an effect on heat tolerance, so it is weaker support for counting the day as a heat day than the hot-water trial.
No safety finding in the abstract; the cautions come from Heathcote 2018 and the consensus.

verification.notes: Added 2026-11-09 for task HT1 (rule I8). Crossref: J Sci Med Sport 10:259-262, 2007-08, four authors, no updated-by notice. Abstract and publication type (clinical trial, cross-over) read on Europe PMC (PMID 16877041). Numbers are the abstract's.
